key_takeaways: Use AI as a drafting partner: write your own memories, habits and promises first, then ask the assistant to shape them rather than write from nothing.
Prompt for options, outlines and a cliché check, and tell it to keep your phrases where it can, so the final vow still sounds like you.
Cut any line a stranger could say about their own partner; our vow guide names soulmate, partner in crime and other half as phrases that belong to everyone.
Our vow guide suggests about 150 words, a minute out loud, with 300 words the most it would suggest; read it aloud with a timer.

In Australia, your own vows sit alongside the legal words, which AI should never rewrite; overseas, an Australian celebrant cannot legally marry you, so confirm the legal steps with the local registrar or embassy.

faq.q: Is it wrong to use AI to write your wedding vows?
faq.a: No, as long as the stories and promises are yours. Use AI to sort and tighten your own notes rather than invent feelings, then edit until no line could belong to a stranger.

faq.q: Should you tell your partner you used AI for your vows?
faq.a: Yes, ideally before either of you starts. Agree together on AI, length and tone, so nobody is surprised at the ceremony and the two vows feel matched.

It can draft them, but only your stories make them yours. A chatbot or vow generator can sort your notes, suggest an order and flag clichés, yet it cannot know your private jokes, your shared history or the promises you mean to keep. Bring that raw material, then edit every line yourself.

faq.q: Is it safe to put personal stories into ChatGPT or another chatbot?
faq.a: Only with care. Use initials, leave out health details and family conflict, and check the tool's data settings first.
